paragraphs.text: Date of hearing 28.10.2026 Petitioner by: Mr. Sajid Mirani, Advocate/Defence counsel at the State expense. State by Mr. Waheed Rafique, Deputy District Public Prosecutor. Complainant by: Mr. Muhammad Arif Cheema, Advocate. Ghulam Sarwar Nihung, J:- The petitioner, Irfan alias Kala, challenges his conviction and sentences under the judgment dated 20.04.2024 passed by the learned Senior Civil Judge (Criminal Division), Khanewal, in case FIR No. 331/2020 dated 17.06.2020, registered under sections 324, 337-A(iv) and 34, PPC, at Police Station Saddar Khanewal. At the conclusion of the trial, the learned trial Court convicted and sentenced him as follows: - “Under Section 324, PPC: To undergo rigorous imprisonment for seven years with fine of Rs.400,000/-, and in default thereof, to further undergo rigorous imprisonment for six months. Under Section 337-A(iv), PPC: To undergo rigorous imprisonment for seven years with fine of Rs.200,000/-, and in default thereof, to further undergo rigorous imprisonment for six months. Under Section 337-D, PPC: To undergo rigorous imprisonment for seven years and to pay Rs.1,439,508/- as Arsh, stated to be 15% of the Diyat amount fixed for the year 2019–2020. Compensation under Section 544-A, Cr.P.C. The petitioner was further directed to pay compensation of Rs.600,000/- to injured Muhammad Ramzan, recoverable as arrears of land revenue, and in default thereof, to further undergo rigorous imprisonment for six months.” All sentences were ordered to run concurrently. The benefit of section 382-B Cr.P.C. was also extended to the convict.

Feeling aggrieved by the judgment of the learned trial Court, Irfan alias Kala, petitioner, preferred a criminal appeal through the Superintendent, District Jail, Khanewal, before the learned Additional Sessions Judge, Khanewal, who (appellate court) vide judgment dated 25.06.2024 upheld the conviction and sentence of the petitioner by dismissing the appeal. Hence, the instant criminal revision before this Court.

Brief facts of the prosecution case, as narrated by Muhammad Asad, complainant, in his complaint (Exh.PA), are that on 17.06.2020, at about 10:45 a.m., his father, Muhammad Ramzan, aged about 60 years, along with Muhammad Akram and Muhammad Imran Ashraf, was sitting at the hotel of Shafiq Chadhar, when Irfan alias Kala, petitioner, along with his co-accused Muhammad Imran, Kamran alias Kama and Ali Raza, arrived there. Two of the co-accused caught hold of Muhammad Ramzan, whereupon the petitioner inflicted a Toka blow on the left side of his head, as a result of which he sustained injury and fell to the ground. On hue and cry raised by the complainant and the witnesses, the accused persons fled away on a motorcycle. The alleged motive behind the occurrence was the marriage of the sister of the accused persons with the brother-in-law of the complainant’s paternal uncle, Haq Nawaz. Consequently, the aforementioned FIR was registered under Sections 324/34, PPC.
Arguments heard. Record perused.

The principal question requiring determination in the instant criminal revision pertains to the fairness of the trial proceedings. A perusal of the record reveals that the statements of PW-1 to PW-3 were recorded on 15.02.2021, that of PW-4 on 11.11.2021, PW-5 on 07.12.2021, PW-6 on 04.01.2022 and PW-7 on 04.10.2023; however, all the said prosecution witnesses were examined-in-chief without being subjected to cross- examination by the defence. The petitioner was then in custody and was not represented by any counsel. The order sheet records that he did not wish to engage a lawyer. A named defence counsel, however, appeared at the stage of recording the petitioner’s statement under section 342, Cr.P.C. The order sheets do not clearly disclose when that counsel entered appearance or when his authority to represent the petitioner was placed on record.

The pivotal questions arising for determination in the instant criminal revision are whether the conduct of the petitioner could be construed as a conscious, voluntary and unequivocal waiver of his right to cross-examine the prosecution witnesses; whether the learned trial Court afforded him a fair, meaningful and effective opportunity to defend himself against the charge; and whether the failure to afford such opportunity occasioned a material procedural irregularity warranting interference by this Court in exercise of its revisional jurisdiction.

The order dated 15.02.2021 passed by the learned Senior Civil Judge (Criminal Division) is material. Its relevant portion is reproduced verbatim: “Today the case was fixed for prosecution evidence. At this stage, accused has been directed to produce his counsel but he is reluctant to produce his counsel before court and further submits he does not want to engage counsel and his case be decided after recording evidence on merits. Statements of PW.1 to PW.3 have been recorded. Opportunity for cross examination was given to the accused but neither he produced his counsel nor he himself conducted cross examination. Official witnesses be summoned through summons for 01.03.2021.” The order in question reflects that the petitioner declined to engage a private counsel and did not cross-examine the prosecution witnesses himself, despite having been afforded an opportunity to do so. However, the question requiring consideration is not whether the petitioner was entitled to repeated adjournments for the purpose of cross-examination, but whether the circumstances recorded by the learned trial Court establish a conscious, informed, voluntary and unequivocal waiver of his valuable right to cross-examine the prosecution witnesses. It is pertinent to observe that refusal to engage a private counsel and voluntary relinquishment of the right to cross-examination are two distinct matters, which cannot be equated with each other. A perusal of the impugned order reveals that it does not reflect that the petitioner was apprised of the legal consequences of foregoing cross-examination or that, having fully understood such consequences, he expressly and voluntarily elected to relinquish the said right.

Article 10-A of the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973, expressly guarantees the right to a fair trial and due process in the following terms: “For the determination of his civil rights and obligations or in any criminal charge against him a person shall be entitled to a fair trial and due process.” The constitutional guarantee of a fair trial is not merely procedural in nature but is a substantive right, which necessarily encompasses a fair, meaningful and effective opportunity for an accused to defend himself against the charge and to challenge the evidence adduced by the prosecution. Furthermore, Article 10(1) of the Constitution provides that: “No person who is arrested shall be detained in custody without being informed, as soon as may be, of the grounds for such arrest, nor shall he be denied the right to consult and be defended by a legal practitioner of his choice.” The right to consult and be defended by a legal practitioner, as enshrined in Article 10(1) of the Constitution, is to be read in conjunction with the constitutional guarantee of a fair trial and due process under Article 10-A of the Constitution. These constitutional safeguards, when read together, underscore the obligation of the trial Court to ensure that an accused is afforded a genuine and effective opportunity to defend himself and that the proceedings are conducted in a manner consistent with the fundamental principles of fairness and due process.

Section 340(1), Cr.P.C. provides: “Any person accused of an offence before a Criminal Court, or against whom proceedings are instituted under this Code in any such Court, may of right be defended by a pleader.” The provision recognizes the accused’s right to be defended by a pleader. In “Muhammad Bashir v. Rukhsar and others” (PLD 2020 SC 334) it has been held that: “The Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan prescribes important safeguards against depriving a person of his “life or liberty” and with regard to arrest and detention, which includes “the right to consult and be defended by a legal practitioner of his choice”. It does not, by its own terms, create an unconditional obligation to provide State funded counsel in every criminal case. The question of legal aid is governed by the applicable law.

The Punjab Legal Aid Act, 2018, provides a statutory mechanism for legal assistance to an indigent person. Section 2 (g) of the Act defines indigent person as “Indigent person” means a person, involved in the commission of an offence or a female involved in a family dispute, and does not have the financial capacity to engage an Advocate on his or her own; Section 9 of the Act provides the procedure for applying to the Agency and determining eligibility. Section 14 of the Act provides: “A court or, as the case may be, an investigating officer, a prosecutor or a prison officer shall, on coming to know that an indigent person remains undefended by an Advocate, shall inform him that he may apply to the Agency for legal aid.” The statutory duty under section 14 of the Act arises when the concerned authority comes to know that an indigent person remains undefended. A perusal of Section 14 of the Punjab Legal Aid Act, 2018, reveals that the legislature has consciously employed the expression “a court” without restricting its scope to any particular category, hierarchy or forum. The said expression, therefore, has to be construed in the light of the definition of “court” contained in Section 2(c) of the Act, which encompasses a court established under any law for the time being in force. Consequently, the statutory obligation contemplated under Section 14 of the Act extends to every court falling within the aforesaid definition. Whenever such court comes to know that an indigent person remains undefended by an Advocate, it is under a mandatory obligation to inform him of his right to apply to the Agency for legal aid. The provision, thus, manifests the legislative intent to ensure that indigence does not, by itself, deprive a person of meaningful access to legal representation. Furthermore, Section 9(7) of the Act preserves the powers otherwise available to a court under any law for the time being in force. Therefore, the statutory scheme cannot be interpreted to curtail an independent power vested in a court to secure legal representation for an indigent person, including through appointment of counsel at State expense, where such power is available under the applicable law. The present record does not show that the petitioner’s financial position was examined or that he was informed of the legal aid mechanism. The trial Court did not clarify whether the petitioner was unable to engage counsel and, if so, whether the statutory procedure was brought to his attention. In “Naubahar alias Baharu v. The State” (2020 YLR 159), this Court examined the right of an accused to be defended through legal counsel, particularly in the context of cross-examination of prosecution witnesses. After considering Articles 10 and 10-A of the Constitution, section 340(1), Cr.P.C., and the relevant Rules and Orders of the Lahore High Court, the Court held that it is the duty of the Court to inform an accused who is unable to afford legal representation of his entitlement to legal assistance at State expense. It further emphasized that the defence counsel must be competent, appointed sufficiently in advance, and provided adequate time and necessary material to prepare the defence. The Court also held that cross-examination conducted personally by an accused cannot be equated with or substituted for cross-examination through a legally trained counsel. Finding that the appellant had been deprived of effective legal assistance at the stage of cross examination of material prosecution witnesses, the Court set aside the conviction and remanded the matter for a fresh decision after affording him an opportunity to cross- examine those witnesses through counsel.

Article 132 of the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984, defines examination-in-chief, cross-examination and re-examination. Article 133(1) provides: “Witnesses shall be first examined-in-chief, then (if the adverse party so desires) cross-examined, then (if the party calling him so desires) re-examined.” Cross-examination enables the adverse party to test the truthfulness, accuracy and reliability of testimony given in examination-in-chief. In Supra Case of Muhammad Bashir, the Honourable Supreme Court held that: “The Constitution also mandates a “fair trial and due process”. A person arrested for an offence: (1) must be informed of the grounds of his arrest; (2) must be permitted to consult with and be defended by a lawyer; (3) must be provided with the information of the offence he is charged for; (4) must be provided with an opportunity to cross-examine witnesses who depose against him; (5) must be given an opportunity to explain the circumstances disclosed in evidence against him; and (6) must also be provided an opportunity to produce evidence in his defence. These are also necessary ingredients to ensure the fairness of a trial. And “The right to cross-examine is the right of the adverse party which right he/she may forego but one which he/she cannot be deprived of.” The principle of fair trial also was reiterated in “Sher Hassan and others v. Gul Hassan Khan and others” (2022 SCMR 1360). A criminal trial must be conducted with utmost fairness and that depriving an accused of the opportunity to cross-examine a witness deposing against him violates the guarantee of fair trial under Article 10-A of the Constitution. The principle is directly applicable: an accused may voluntarily forego cross- examination, but the Court cannot deprive him of that opportunity. Whether the right was voluntarily abandoned must be determined from the circumstances appearing on the judicial record.

The order dated 15.02.2021 passed by learned Senior Civil Judge (Criminal Division), Khanewal does not establish such a waiver. It records the petitioner’s unwillingness to engage a private lawyer and his statement that the case may be decided after recording of evidence. It does not record that he was asked whether he wished to cross-examine the witnesses personally, whether he understood the evidentiary consequences of not doing so, or whether he wished to relinquish that right despite being informed of those consequences. Nor does it disclose whether the petitioner’s ability to arrange counsel was ascertained. The mere recording that an opportunity was given cannot, in these circumstances, be treated as conclusive proof of an informed waiver.

The subsequent proceedings do not cure the omission. On 28.02.2024, when the petitioner’s statement under section 342, Cr.P.C. was recorded, the appearance of Mian Samir Abbas Sial Faqir, Advocate, was entered in the order sheet. The available order sheets do not clearly disclose when the counsel entered appearance, when his vakalatnama was filed, or whether and when it was accepted. This Court does not presume that no vakalatnama was filed merely because the relevant entry is absent from the order sheet. The omission is, however, material because the petitioner was unrepresented when the prosecution witnesses were examined, whereas counsel appeared at a later stage. A clear order sheet should record the filing and acceptance of a vakalatnama or, where counsel is appointed through legal aid or under another lawful mechanism, the basis of that appointment.

Section 342(1), Cr.P.C. provides: “For the purpose of enabling the accused to explain any circumstances appearing in the evidence against him, the Court may, at any stage of any inquiry or trial without previously warning the accused, put such questions to him as the Court considers necessary, and shall, for the purpose aforesaid, question him generally on the case after the witnesses for the prosecution have been examined and before he is called on for his defence.” The object of section 342, Cr.P.C. is to enable the accused to explain the circumstances appearing against him. It does not provide a substitute for cross examination, which serves the separate purpose of testing the prosecution evidence. In answer to question No. 9 of his statement under section 342, Cr.P.C., the petitioner stated as under:- “I am innocent. I have not granted opportunity to cross examine the witnesses due to which prosecution evidence is incomplete and not reliable. Kindly acquit me.” The petitioner thus raised the issue of non-cross-examination during the trial itself. His statement does not, by itself, determine whether the earlier omission was lawful, but it confirms that the matter was not raised for the first time before this Court.

The cumulative effect of the record is, therefore, significant. The petitioner was in custody and unrepresented by counsel when the prosecution witnesses were examined; no cross-examination was conducted; the order sheet does not reflect any informed and unequivocal waiver of the right to cross-examination; nor does the record indicate that his ability to engage counsel or his eligibility for legal aid was examined; and the subsequent appearance of counsel is not clearly documented. The petitioner also complained of the absence of an opportunity to cross- examine in his statement under section 342, Cr.P.C. Considered together, these circumstances disclose a material deficiency in the conduct of the trial.

This Court is not holding that every omission in an order sheet vitiates a trial, that every accused who declines to engage private counsel must be granted repeated adjournments, or that the absence of a recorded vakalatnama automatically renders a later appearance unauthorized. Nor does the law permit an accused to obstruct proceedings by deliberate non- cooperation. The finding in the present case rests on the particular combination of circumstances and, above all, the absence of a clear record showing that the petitioner knowingly and voluntarily abandoned cross examination.

A careful examination of the judgment dated 25.06.2024, passed by the learned appellate Court, reveals that the conviction and sentences awarded to the petitioner were maintained primarily on the strength of the prosecution evidence, which had remained unchallenged for want of cross- examination. The learned appellate Court, while observing that the petitioner had failed to cross-examine the prosecution witnesses, proceeded to treat their statements as correct and upheld the conviction without examining whether the petitioner had consciously, voluntarily and unequivocally waived his valuable right of cross-examination or had been afforded a fair and effective opportunity to defend himself. Thus, the learned appellate Court failed to appreciate the material procedural deficiency affecting the fairness of the trial. In this regard, Section 423(1)(b)(i), Cr.P.C., empowers the appellate Court, in an appeal against conviction, to reverse the finding and sentence and either acquit or discharge the accused or order his retrial by a Court of competent jurisdiction subordinate to the appellate Court. In the peculiar circumstances of the instant case, the mere failure to cross-examine the prosecution witnesses does not, by itself, furnish a ground for acquittal of the petitioner; however, the conviction and sentences recorded against him cannot safely be maintained without first curing the aforesaid procedural defect, which goes to the very root of a fair trial. Consequently, the appropriate course would be to set aside the judgments of both the Courts below and remand the case to the learned trial Court for retrial from the stage of prosecution evidence, with a direction to afford the petitioner a fair, meaningful and effective opportunity to cross-examine the prosecution witnesses through counsel and thereafter proceed with the trial strictly in accordance with law.

The learned trial Court shall afford the petitioner a reasonable opportunity to engage counsel of his choice. If he states that he cannot afford counsel, the Court shall ascertain whether he is an indigent person within the meaning of the Punjab Legal Aid Act, 2018, and, if so, inform him of his right to apply to the Punjab Legal Aid Agency under section 14 of the Act and proceed in accordance with the applicable procedure. If, after being duly informed and afforded a reasonable opportunity, the petitioner voluntarily declines legal assistance or cross-examination, the Court shall record his statement and the circumstances clearly and proceed in accordance with law. The petitioner shall not be permitted to frustrate the proceedings through deliberate or unreasonable conduct. The trial Court shall also ensure that the appearance of every defence counsel, and the filing and acceptance of the vakalatnama or other lawful basis of representation, are properly reflected in the order sheet. Unnecessary adjournments shall be avoided and the proceedings shall be concluded expeditiously.

For the reasons recorded above, the instant revision petition is allowed. The judgment of conviction and sentence dated 20.04.2024 passed by the learned Senior Civil Judge (Criminal Division), Khanewal, and the judgment dated 25.06.2024 passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge, Khanewal, are set aside. The case is remanded to the learned trial Court for retrial from the stage of prosecution evidence, in accordance with the directions contained in this judgment. No opinion is expressed on the merits of the prosecution case.

The record of the case be transmitted to the learned trial Court forthwith. The parties shall appear before the learned trial Court on the date to be fixed by it. (Ghulam Sarwar Nihung) Judge Approved for reporting. Judge Announced, dictated, prepared and signed on 28.10.2026. *M.Fayyaz*
